title: I Built an Open-Source McDonald's Meal Recommender Using MCP and Python
author: echo lee
summary: Why I Built McPilot Choosing what to eat sounds simple, but finding a meal that fits your budget, nutritional goals, and taste preferences can be surprisingly complicated. I built McPilot , an open-source McDonald's meal recommendation assistant powered by the official McDonald's China MCP (Model Context Protocol) service. Instead of generating arbitrary suggestions, McPilot uses available menu, store, nutrition, and coupon information to create explainable meal recommendations. What Does It Do? McPilot supports three recommendation strategies: Budget First: Finds more affordable meal combinations within a specified budget. High Protein: Prioritizes meals with better protein content when reliable nutritional information is available. Balanced Recommendation: Considers price, nutrition, personal preferences, and meal composition. Users can provide their budget, party size, dietary restrictions, and nutritional goals. The system also supports price calculations, explanations for its recommendations, missing-data warnings, and suggestions when no suitable meal combination is found. How It Works McPilot combines several components: McDonald's China MCP: Provides access to supported restaurant, menu, nutrition, and coupon information. Python: Handles data processing, validation, and recommendation logic. Tencent WorkBuddy: An AI coding assistant used during development, debugging, and Skill creation. Responsive Web Interface: Allows users to enter preferences and view recommendations on desktop or mobile devices. GitHub: Hosts the open-source code and documentation. The project communicates with the MCP service through Streamable HTTP. All MCP operations are read-only. McPilot does not place orders, claim coupons, or perform transactions. Screenshots Main Interface McPilot's main interface allows users to configure their meal preferences. Recommendation Results The application presents different meal recommendations based on the selected strategy. Mobile Interface The interface is also designed for smaller screens. Lessons Learned One challenge was handling incomplete nutritional information. If an item has no reliable protein or calorie data, the system should not automatically treat the missing value as zero. McPilot explicitly identifies missing data to avoid misleading recommendations. Another important consideration was explainability. Rather than only showing a meal combination, the application aims to explain why it was recommended. Limitations McPilot currently integrates with McDonald's China MCP , so its data availability and supported ordering scenarios are specific to that service. Using the live MCP functionality requires appropriate access and configuration. The project is a recommendation tool, not a global McDonald's ordering service. Open Source The repository includes the Python implementation, WorkBuddy Skill, MCP integration documentation, configuration examples, and usage instructions. GitHub Repository: McPilot — Open-Source Meal Recommender McPilot has also been accepted as an entry in the 2026 McDonald's Developer Innovation Challenge. If you're interested in MCP, AI agents, or recommendation systems, feel free to explore the code and share feedback. If you find it useful, a GitHub Star is appreciated! Final Thoughts McPilot is an experiment in bringing AI-assisted development and real-world MCP data together to solve a small everyday problem. The goal is not simply to generate meal suggestions, but to make recommendations more transparent, data-driven, and practical.

title: CBT Techniques for Developer Burnout: How to Reframe 'I'm Not Productive Enough
author: CBT Tools
summary:
If you've ever stared at your IDE at 2 PM, brain fogged, and thought "I'm not productive enough" , you're not alone. Developer burnout is at record highs — and the inner monologue that drives it is remarkably predictable. The good news? That inner monologue follows patterns. And patterns can be hacked. This tutorial shows you how to use Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) techniques — the same evidence-based methods therapists use — to identify and reframe the cognitive distortions that fuel developer burnout. We'll build a simple Python tool along the way. What Is CBT (And Why Should Developers Care)? CBT is a structured, evidence-based therapy that works by identifying the cognitive distortions — systematic errors in thinking — that drive negative emotions. For developers, these distortions often manifest as: "I should be shipping faster" (Should statements) "One bad PR review means I'm a bad engineer" (All-or-nothing thinking) "Everyone else is more productive than me" (Comparison distortion) "If I don't work this weekend, I'll fall behind forever" (Catastrophizing) CBT gives you a structured way to catch these thoughts, examine the evidence, and reframe them. Think of it as debugging for your brain . The CBT Thought Record: Your Mental Debug Log The core CBT tool is the Thought Record — a structured log where you: Situation : What triggered the thought? Automatic Thought : What did your brain say? Emotion : What did you feel? (0-100 intensity) Cognitive Distortion : Which thinking error is this? Evidence For : What supports the thought? Evidence Against : What contradicts it? Balanced Thought : A fair, evidence-based reframe New Emotion : How do you feel now? (0-100) Let's build one in Python. Building a CBT Thought Record Tool in Python from dataclasses import dataclass , field from datetime import datetime from typing import Optional import json @dataclass class ThoughtRecord : """ A single CBT thought record entry. """ situation : str automatic_thought : str emotion : str emotion_intensity : int # 0-100 cognitive_distortion : str evidence_for : str evidence_against : str balanced_thought : str new_emotion_intensity : int # 0-100 timestamp : str = field ( default_factory = lambda : datetime . now (). isoformat ()) # Common developer cognitive distortions DEVELOPER_DISTORTIONS = { " all_or_nothing " : " All-or-nothing thinking: one failure = total failure " , " catastrophizing " : " Catastrophizing: assuming the worst possible outcome " , " should_statements " : " Should statements: rigid rules about how you ' should ' perform " , " comparison " : " Comparison distortion: comparing your inside to others ' outside " , " personalization " : " Personalization: taking blame for things outside your control " , " mental_filter " : " Mental filter: focusing only on negatives, filtering out positives " , " labeling " : " Labeling: ' I am a bad engineer ' instead of ' I made a mistake '" , } def create_thought_record () -> ThoughtRecord : """ Interactive CLI to create a thought record. """ print ( " === CBT Thought Record === 
 " ) situation = input ( " What situation triggered the thought? 
 > " ) auto_thought = input ( " 
 What did your brain automatically say? 
 > " ) emotion = input ( " 
 What emotion did you feel? (e.g., anxiety, guilt, shame) 
 > " ) intensity = int ( input ( " 
 Intensity 0-100? 
 > " )) print ( " 
 Common developer distortions: " ) for key , desc in DEVELOPER_DISTORTIONS . items (): print ( f " { key } : { desc } " ) distortion = input ( " 
 Which distortion matches? 
 > " ) evidence_for = input ( " 
 Evidence FOR the thought: 
 > " ) evidence_against = input ( " 
 Evidence AGAINST the thought: 
 > " ) balanced = input ( " 
 Balanced reframe: 
 > " ) new_intensity = int ( input ( " 
 New emotion intensity 0-100? 
 > " )) return ThoughtRecord ( situation = situation , automatic_thought = auto_thought , emotion = emotion , emotion_intensity = intensity , cognitive_distortion = distortion , evidence_for = evidence_for , evidence_against = evidence_against , balanced_thought = balanced , new_emotion_intensity = new_intensity , ) # Example: Developer burnout thought record example = ThoughtRecord ( situation = " PR got 3 change requests on code I worked on all week " , automatic_thought = " I ' m not productive enough. I should have gotten it right the first time. " , emotion = " shame " , emotion_intensity = 75 , cognitive_distortion = " should_statements " , evidence_for = " The PR did need changes. " , evidence_against = " Change requests are normal. I shipped 4 other PRs this week that merged cleanly. Senior devs get change requests too. Code review is collaborative, not a test. " , balanced_thought = " Change requests are part of the process, not a verdict on my worth. I can address the feedback and learn from it. " , new_emotion_intensity = 30 , ) print ( json . dumps ( example . __dict__ , indent = 2 )) Run this and you'll see the emotional intensity drop from 75 → 30 — just by examining the evidence. The 6 Burnout Thought Patterns (And How to Reframe Them) Developer burnout has six characteristic thought patterns. Here's each one with its reframe: 1. "I'm Not Productive Enough" Distortion : Comparison + Should statements Reframe : "Productivity is not a single metric. I shipped working code, helped in code review, and unblocked a teammate. That's a productive day." 2. "Everyone Else Ships Faster Than Me" Distortion : Comparison distortion (comparing your inside to their outside) Reframe : "I see their merged PRs, not their WIP branches, reverts, and debug sessions. I don't have their full picture." 3. "If I Rest, I'll Fall Behind" Distortion : Catastrophizing Reframe : "Taking a break today costs ~2 hours. Burning out costs ~2 months. The math favors rest." 4. "My Worth = My Output" Distortion : Labeling / All-or-nothing Reframe : "I am a person who writes code, among many other things. My worth is not a function of my commit count." 5. "I Should Be Able to Handle This" Distortion : Should statements Reframe : "Burnout is a well-documented occupational phenomenon (ICD-11). It's not a personal failure. It's a signal that something in the environment needs to change." 6. "It's Too Late to Change Anything" Distortion : All-or-nothing + Catastrophizing Reframe : "I can change one thing today: take a lunch break, set a boundary, log off at 6. Small changes compound." Automating the Reframe: A Distortion Detector import re # Pattern → distortion mapping BURNTOUT_PATTERNS = { r " not (productive|shipping|fast) enough " : " comparison " , r " everyone else (is|does|ships) " : " comparison " , r " i should (be|have|not) " : " should_statements " , r " (always|never|forever|impossible) " : " all_or_nothing " , r " if i (rest|stop|take a break) " : " catastrophizing " , r " i am (a |an )?(bad|failure|fraud|imposter) " : " labeling " , r " (too late|no point|what ' s the use) " : " all_or_nothing " , } def detect_distortions ( journal_entry : str ) -> list [ tuple [ str , str ]]: """ Scan a journal entry for cognitive distortions. """ entry_lower = journal_entry . lower () found = [] for pattern , distortion in BURNTOUT_PATTERNS . items (): matches = re . findall ( pattern , entry_lower ) if matches : found . append (( distortion , matches )) return found # Test it journal = """ I ' m not productive enough today. Everyone else ships faster. I should be able to handle this workload. If I rest, I ' ll fall behind. It ' s too late to change anything. """ distortions = detect_distortions ( journal ) for d , matches in distortions : print ( f " ⚠️ { d } : { matches } " ) Output: ⚠️ comparison: ['productive', 'ships'] ⚠️ should_statements: ['be'] ⚠️ catastrophizing: ['rest'] ⚠️ all_or_nothing: ['too late'] The Behavioral Experiment: Testing Your Beliefs CBT isn't just thinking differently — it's testing whether your beliefs are accurate. For developers, this means running behavioral experiments: @dataclass class BehavioralExperiment : """ Test a burnout belief against reality. """ belief : str prediction : str # What you think will happen experiment : str # What you'll do actual_outcome : str = "" belief_confirmed : Optional [ bool ] = None def record_outcome ( self , outcome : str ): self . actual_outcome = outcome # Did reality match the prediction? self . belief_confirmed = outcome . lower () in self . prediction . lower () # Example: "If I log off at 6 PM, my team will think I'm lazy" experiment = BehavioralExperiment ( belief = " If I log off at 6 PM, my team will think I ' m lazy " , prediction = " Team will comment on my early departure or reduce my responsibilities " , experiment = " Log off at 6 PM for 3 days. Observe team reactions. " , ) # After 3 days: experiment . record_outcome ( " No one commented. One teammate said ' good boundaries ' . PR merged normally next morning. " ) print ( f " Belief confirmed: { experiment . belief_confirmed } " ) print ( f " The belief was WRONG. Logging off at 6 is safe. " ) Free Interactive CBT Tools I've built a set of free, privacy-first CBT tools that run entirely in your browser — no signup, no backend, no data collection: 🔗 CBT Toolkit on GitHub The toolkit includes: Interactive thought record builder Cognitive distortion reference with developer-specific examples CBT techniques for 50+ specific conditions (anxiety, burnout, imposter syndrome, perfectionism) All vanilla JavaScript, all open source When to Seek Professional Help CBT self-help tools are powerful, but they're not a substitute for professional therapy. Seek help if: Burnout symptoms persist > 2 weeks despite self-help You experience thoughts of self-harm Burnout is affecting your physical health (sleep, appetite, chest pain) You're using substances to cope Resources : 988 (US Suicide & Crisis Lifeline — call or text) Your company's EAP (Employee Assistance Program) Psychology Today's therapist finder (psychologytoday.com) Summary Developer burnout is driven by predictable cognitive distortions. CBT gives you structured tools to: Catch the automatic thought (Thought Record) Identify the distortion (Pattern matching) Examine the evidence (For and against) Reframe to a balanced perspective Test with behavioral experiments The thought record takes 5 minutes. The payoff is shifting from "I'm not productive enough" to "I'm doing sustainable work at a sustainable pace" — and actually believing it. This tutorial is educational, not medical advice. If you're struggling, please reach out to a mental health professional or call 988. title: The Farmer's AI-Advisor
author: Dilesh Zingare
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built The Farmer's AI-Advisor is a specialized, offline agricultural assistant built specifically for farmers in the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra, India . Unlike standard cloud-dependent AI tools, this assistant operates completely offline without an internet connection . Because many remote farmlands lack stable network access, this architecture ensures that critical agricultural guidance is always available when and where it is needed most. How it works: Location & Time Filtering: The user selects their specific Vidarbha district and the current month. Context-Aware Querying: The farmer asks a question regarding crop choices, ideal sowing windows, or pest/insecticide control. Offline Intelligence: The application uses localized historical agricultural reference data combined with local AI inference to provide language-accurate advice without hallucinating information. Demo 📺 Watch the video demonstration here: YouTube Link Code 💻 Explore the open-source repository: GitHub - The Farmer's AI Friend How I Built It Resource constraints drive genuine engineering innovations. My personal laptop only has 5.9 GB of usable RAM , leaving roughly 1–3 GB free for active development. To make a fully local AI application run smoothly under these strict hardware limits, I built the orchestration layer using Python and Streamlit , and deployed Google’s Gemma 3:1b open-weight model locally using Ollama . The Technical Stack: LLM Engine: gemma3:1b running locally via Ollama (highly optimized for low-resource hardware processing). User Interface: Streamlit (providing a lightweight, interactive web UI framework). Voice Processing: faster-whisper for offline local voice recognition, enabling hands-free operation for farmers out in the field. Knowledge Guardrails: A structured JSON-based dataset ( advice.json ) containing localized crop parameters to steer the model and completely prevent inaccurate fabrications. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? As a developer under 18, I hit a massive roadblock trying to build with proprietary AI platforms: closed-source ecosystems require credit cards and restrict access to minors. Furthermore, commercial API paywalls are entirely unaffordable for students trying to build impact-driven projects. Open-source and open-weight models level the playing field. They prove that AI belongs to everyone —not just tech giants or those with massive credit limits. Open innovation allows student developers like me to build high-impact applications that can actively change lives, shaping the future technological landscape of our communities. Prize Categories I am entering The Farmer's AI-Advisor into the following official Hacktoberfest challenge categories: Best Use of Gemma (Featured Category): This system is natively engineered around Google's open-weight gemma3:1b model. By optimizing the application to operate fluidly on a consumer-grade 6GB RAM student laptop, it showcases the democratization of AI on everyday hardware. Overall Best Open-Source AI Project: This application serves as an impact-driven, offline utility designed specifically to break down digital, financial, and connectivity barriers within global agricultural communities. summary: 最近不少朋友在做新兴市场的量化策略，印度股市是绕不开的一个。NSE（印度国家证券交易所）和BSE（孟买证券交易所）的市值加起来排全球前列，而且增长速度快，很多策略在印度市场的表现跟美股完全不一样。 但接印度股票数据的时候，有几个跟美股、港股都不一样的地方——尤其是订阅格式和交易所指定。这篇记录一下接入印度股票行情的全过程。 印度市场跟其他市场有什么不一样 刚开始接的时候我以为跟美股一样，直接传个代码和region就行，结果发现根本不是那么回事。 第一，印度有两个主要交易所：NSE和BSE。 同一只股票在两个交易所都可能上市，代码一样但交易所不同。所以接印度股票的时候，必须指定交易所，不然返回的数据可能不是你想要的那个。 第二，WebSocket订阅格式不一样。 美股是两个参数： AAPL$US （代码$市场）。印度是三个参数： RELIANCE$NSE$IN （代码$交易所$市场）。一开始我按美股的格式传，结果订阅一直失败。 第三，region代码是 IN 。 不是 US 、 HK 那种，印度市场传 IN 。 REST拉取印度股票报价 先从REST开始，确认数据格式对不对。 import requests API_BASE = " https://api.itick.org " TOKEN = " your_token_here " headers = { " accept " : " application/json " , " token " : TOKEN } # 拉几只印度大盘股 stocks = [ ( " RELIANCE " , " NSE " ), # 信实工业 ( " TCS " , " NSE " ), # 塔塔咨询 ( " INFY " , " NSE " ), # 印孚瑟斯 ] for code , exchange in stocks : q = get_india_stock_quote ( code , exchange ) sign = " + " if q [ " chp " ] >= 0 else "" print ( f " { code } ( { exchange } ): { q [ ' ld ' ] } ( { sign }{ q [ ' chp ' ] } %) " ) 返回字段跟其他市场基本一致： ld 最新价、 chp 涨跌幅、 o/h/l 开高低、 v 成交量。做行情看板这些字段够用了。 注意 ：印度股票的代码是字母形式（RELIANCE、TCS），不是数字。跟港股的数字代码（700）不一样。 WebSocket订阅印度股票（重点） 这是印度市场最容易踩坑的地方——订阅格式跟其他市场不一样。 其他市场（美股、港股、外汇）都是两个参数： 代码$市场 ，比如 AAPL$US 。 印度市场是三个参数： 代码$交易所$市场 ，比如 RELIANCE$NSE$IN 。 import json import threading import time import websocket WS_URL = " wss://api.itick.org/stock " TOKEN = " your_token_here " authenticated = False def on_message ( ws , message ): global authenticated payload = json . loads ( message ) # 先等鉴权成功 if payload . get ( " resAc " ) == " auth " and payload . get ( " code " ) == 1 and not authenticated : authenticated = True # 印度股票订阅格式：代码$交易所$市场 ws . send ( json . dumps ({ " ac " : " subscribe " , " params " : " RELIANCE$NSE$IN,TCS$NSE$IN " , " types " : " quote " })) return if payload . get ( " resAc " ) == " pong " : return data = payload . get ( " data " ) or {} if data . get ( " type " ) == " quote " : sign = " + " if data [ " chp " ] >= 0 else "" print ( f " { data [ ' s ' ] } : { data [ ' ld ' ] } ( { sign }{ data [ ' chp ' ] } %) " ) 为什么印度要多一个交易所参数？ 因为同一只股票在NSE和BSE都可能上市，价格可能不一样。指定交易所才能确保你拿到的是你想要的那个交易所的数据。 K线数据获取 K线接口跟其他市场一样，只是多了个exchange参数。 def get_india_kline ( code , exchange = " NSE " , k_type = 8 , limit = 100 ): """ k_type: 1=1分钟 2=5分钟 5=1小时 8=日K 9=周K 10=月K """ resp = requests . get ( f " { API_BASE } /stock/kline " , headers = headers , params = { " region " : " IN " , " code " : code , " exchange " : exchange , " kType " : k_type , " limit " : limit } ) return resp . json ()[ " data " ] # WebSocketApp ( WS_URL , header = [ f " token: { TOKEN } " ], on_message = on_message ) ws . run_forever () 这个脚本跑起来之后，开盘前先看到一组印度股票的快照，盘中实时更新价格和涨跌幅。 小结 接印度股票数据的技术框架跟美股、港股差不多——REST做快照和历史数据，WebSocket做实时推送。但有几个特殊点：订阅格式是三个参数（代码$交易所$市场）、必须指定NSE或BSE交易所、交易时间跟国内有时差。这些细节不踩一遍坑很容易忽略。 参考文档： https://docs.itick.org/websocket/stocks GitHub： https://github.com/itick-org/

title: How to Build an Airdrop Monitor with AI — 2026-10-10 #4
author: Nexus Intelligence Research
summary: Monitoring crypto airdrops manually is inefficient and prone to error. Traditional scripts often fail to adapt to dynamic front-end changes or complex eligibility criteria. By integrating Artificial Intelligence, you can build a robust, self-healing Airdrop Monitor that understands context, not just patterns. This guide demonstrates how to leverage LLMs to automate the detection and verification of airdrop opportunities. The Core Architecture A standard airdrop monitor consists of three layers: Data Ingestion, AI Analysis, and Action Execution. The AI layer is critical because airdrop pages are rarely static; they change layouts, add new tasks, or obscure information behind JavaScript. Instead of brittle CSS selectors, use your AI API to parse the rendered HTML and extract structured data.
